question:
Choose the option which is similar in meaning to the underlined word.

He did his work reluctantly because he did not like the director.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Perfunctorily.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Reluctantly means unwillingly; doing something without interest or enthusiasm. (अनिच्छा से / बेमन से)

 

• Perfunctorily means doing something with minimum effort, carelessly and without real interest — as a mere routine. (बेमन से / औपचारिकता निभाते हुए)

 

• The clue 'because he did not like the director' shows he worked half-heartedly, so 'perfunctorily' best fits the sense of the underlined word.
◦  Example: He glanced perfunctorily at the report and signed it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Voluntarily): 'Voluntarily' means of one's own free will, willingly — the opposite of reluctantly.

 

• Option 3 (Enthusiastically): 'Enthusiastically' means with great eagerness — a clear antonym of reluctantly.

 

• Option 4 (Thankfully): 'Thankfully' means with gratitude, or 'fortunately' — unrelated to the sense of unwillingness.

 

• Synonyms of reluctantly: unwillingly, grudgingly, half-heartedly, hesitantly, perfunctorily. Antonyms: willingly, eagerly, readily, enthusiastically.

 

NOTE

 

• Related forms: reluctant (adj.), reluctance (noun). Perfunctory (adj.) = done as a routine duty with little care.

question:
Choose a word that is similar in meaning to the word in bold.

The young journalist jeopardized her career to save the lives of many slum children.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Endangered.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jeopardize means to put someone or something into a situation where there is a risk of loss, harm or failure. (खतरे में डालना)

 

• Endangered means put in danger — an exact synonym of jeopardized.

 

• The journalist risked her career to save the children, i.e. she endangered her career.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Safeguarded): 'Safeguarded' means protected from harm — the opposite of jeopardized.

 

• Option 2 (Rejuvenated): 'Rejuvenated' means made to look or feel younger/fresh again — unrelated.

 

• Option 4 (Celebrated): 'Celebrated' means publicly honoured or praised — unrelated to risk.

 

• Synonyms of jeopardize: endanger, imperil, threaten, risk, expose, compromise. Antonyms: protect, safeguard, secure, shield.

 

NOTE

 

• Noun form: jeopardy (danger). Phrase: 'in jeopardy' = at risk. Spelling: j-e-o-p-a-r-d-i-z-e (British: jeopardise).

question:
Choose a word that is similar in meaning to the word in bold.

Although Mona has a slight speech impediment, she still speaks confidently in front of people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Defect.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Impediment means a hindrance or obstruction; in the phrase 'speech impediment' it means a defect in a person's speech, such as a stammer or lisp. (रुकावट / दोष)

 

• Defect means a shortcoming, imperfection or flaw — the correct synonym in this context.

 

• Though Mona has a slight speech defect, she still speaks confidently.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Advancement): 'Advancement' means progress or promotion — the opposite of a hindrance.

 

• Option 3 (Imposition): 'Imposition' means the act of forcing something on someone, or an unfair burden — not a speech flaw.

 

• Option 4 (Advantage): 'Advantage' means a favourable condition — an antonym of impediment.

 

• Synonyms of impediment: hindrance, obstacle, obstruction, barrier, handicap, defect. Antonyms: aid, help, assistance, advantage, benefit.

 

NOTE

 

• Related verb: impede (to obstruct). Do not confuse 'impediment' with 'impedimenta' (baggage/equipment carried by an army).

question:
Choose the word which conveys the OPPOSITE meaning for the word “Feisty”

Both the magicians were frisky, feisty and full of tricks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. cowardly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Feisty means spirited, lively, determined and courageous; full of fight. (साहसी / जोशीला)

 

• Its opposite is cowardly — lacking courage, timid and easily frightened. (कायर)

 

• In the sentence, 'frisky, feisty and full of tricks' describes bold and energetic magicians; the antonym 'cowardly' reverses this quality.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Sorrow): 'Sorrow' is a noun meaning sadness — it is not an adjective and is not the opposite of feisty.

 

• Option 2 (dauntless): 'Dauntless' means fearless and determined — a synonym of feisty, not an antonym.

 

• Option 3 (plucky): 'Plucky' means brave and spirited — also a synonym of feisty.

 

• Synonyms of feisty: spirited, spunky, plucky, gutsy, bold, courageous. Antonyms: cowardly, timid, meek, spineless, faint-hearted.

 

NOTE

 

• In antonym questions, first eliminate synonyms (here dauntless, plucky) and words of a different part of speech (sorrow).

question:
Choose the word which has the opposite meaning to the given word :

LASSITUDE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. enthusiasm.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lassitude means a state of physical or mental weariness; lack of energy. (थकावट / सुस्ती)

 

• Its opposite is enthusiasm — intense eagerness, energy and interest. (उत्साह)

 

• A person suffering from lassitude lacks energy, whereas an enthusiastic person is full of it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (pleasure): 'Pleasure' means enjoyment or happiness — it is not the direct opposite of weariness.

 

• Option 2 (lustrous): 'Lustrous' means shining or glossy — unrelated to energy levels.

 

• Option 3 (lethargy): 'Lethargy' means sluggishness and lack of energy — a synonym of lassitude, not an antonym.

 

• Synonyms of lassitude: lethargy, weariness, fatigue, languor, listlessness, torpor. Antonyms: energy, vigour, vitality, liveliness, enthusiasm.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse lassitude (tiredness) with latitude (freedom of action; also a geographical term).

question:
Choose the one word substitute for the below sentence.

Mark asked his uncle, a place where ships are docked for maintenance called?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dockyard.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A dockyard is an area with docks and equipment where ships are built, repaired and maintained. (पोत-निर्माण / मरम्मत स्थल)

 

• The sentence asks for a place where ships are 'docked for maintenance' — this is exactly a dockyard.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Harbour): 'Harbour' is a sheltered area of water where ships can anchor safely — not specifically for maintenance.

 

• Option 3 (Port): 'Port' is a town or place with a harbour where ships load and unload cargo/passengers.

 

• Option 4 (Wharf): 'Wharf' is a level structure built along the shore where ships are moored to load and unload.

 

• Dry dock: a narrow basin that can be drained so the ship's hull can be repaired. Shipyard: place where ships are built and repaired (close synonym of dockyard). Quay: a stone platform alongside water for loading ships.

 

NOTE

 

• One-word substitution questions test precise meaning — look for the key phrase ('for maintenance') that separates the correct word from near-synonyms.

question:
Choose the one word substitute for the below sentence.

Aditya waited patiently in the small room that served as the entrance to a much larger space.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Anteroom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An anteroom is a small room leading into a larger, more important room; a waiting room or entrance chamber. (प्रतीक्षा-कक्ष / उपकक्ष)

 

• Prefix 'ante-' means 'before' — the room that comes before the main room.

 

• Aditya waited in the small room that served as the entrance to a larger space, i.e. the anteroom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Bedroom): 'Bedroom' is a room for sleeping — not an entrance room.

 

• Option 3 (Kitchen): 'Kitchen' is a room where food is prepared.

 

• Option 4 (Bathroom): 'Bathroom' is a room with a bath/toilet — none of these serves as an entrance chamber.

 

• Similar words: antechamber, vestibule, foyer, lobby. Other 'ante-' words: antedate, antecedent, antenatal, ante meridiem (a.m.).

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse ante- (before) with anti- (against), e.g. antechamber vs antibiotic.

question:
Choose the one word substitute for the below sentence.

The term for something that causes sexual arousal is called:
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Aphrodisiac.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An aphrodisiac is a food, drink or drug that stimulates sexual desire. (कामोत्तेजक पदार्थ)

 

• The word comes from Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Antiseptic): 'Antiseptic' is a substance that prevents the growth of disease-causing micro-organisms.

 

• Option 3 (Antidote): 'Antidote' is a medicine taken to counteract a poison.

 

• Option 4 (Antonym): 'Antonym' is a word opposite in meaning to another word.

 

• Related one-word substitutes: Anaesthetic — substance causing loss of sensation; Analgesic — pain-killer; Placebo — a harmless pill given for psychological effect; Antibiotic — drug that kills bacteria.

 

NOTE

 

• Many one-word substitutes are derived from Greek/Roman mythology: aphrodisiac (Aphrodite), panic (Pan), narcissism (Narcissus), tantalize (Tantalus).

question:
Identify the grammatical error in the sentence below.

The people here have nothing. Their poverty’s extreme.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. poverty’s.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is in poverty’s. Here the contraction 'poverty’s' stands for 'poverty is'.

 

• In formal/standard written English, a noun + 'is' should not be contracted in this way; also 'poverty’s' looks like a possessive form, which creates ambiguity.

 

• Correct sentence: The people here have nothing. Their poverty is extreme.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (extreme): 'extreme' is correctly used as an adjective (complement) describing the degree of poverty.

 

• Option 3 (people): 'people' is correctly used as a plural noun with the plural verb 'have'.

 

• Option 4 (nothing): 'nothing' is correctly used as the object of 'have'.

 

• Contractions such as it’s, he’s, they’re are informal and common with pronouns; with ordinary nouns (poverty’s, John’s = John is) they are avoided in formal writing because the apostrophe-s normally shows possession.

 

• 'People' is plural and always takes a plural verb: The people are / have.

 

NOTE

 

• In SSC error-spotting, a contraction that can be mistaken for a possessive is usually treated as the error part.

question:
Identify the grammatical error in the sentence below.

The palace is heavily guarded, because inside it’s walls sit the European leaders.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. inside it’s walls.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is in inside it’s walls. It’s = 'it is' / 'it has', whereas the possessive form of 'it' is its (no apostrophe). (इसका)

 

• Correct sentence: The palace is heavily guarded, because inside its walls sit the European leaders.

 

• The sentence uses inversion ('inside its walls sit the European leaders') which is grammatically acceptable.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (palace is): 'palace is' — singular subject with singular verb; correct.

 

• Option 3 (European leaders): 'European leaders' — correct; 'European' begins with a 'yu' sound, and the plural noun agrees with 'sit'.

 

• Option 4 (heavily guarded): 'heavily guarded' — adverb 'heavily' correctly modifies the participle 'guarded'.

 

• Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, hers, ours, yours, theirs, whose.

 

• Contractions: it’s = it is/it has; who’s = who is; they’re = they are; you’re = you are.

 

NOTE

 

• Quick test: replace 'it’s' with 'it is' — if the sentence becomes meaningless ('inside it is walls'), the correct form is 'its'.

question: Identify the incorrect sentence.
option_1: Mitali's hair is long and black.
option_2: Either of the alternatives seems to present major difficulties.
option_3: One of the cars in the garage is fifty years old.
option_4: Sharon has shared her devastating grief after the sudden death of her 57-year-old brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Either of the alternatives seems to present major difficulties.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Either' means 'one or the other of two'. It is used when a choice is to be made between two things, and it takes a singular verb.

 

• The sentence intends to say that both/each of the alternatives present major difficulties, not merely 'one or the other'. Hence the use of 'either' is logically incorrect here.

 

• Correct form: Each of the alternatives seems to present major difficulties. / Both (of the) alternatives seem to present major difficulties.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Mitali's hair is long and black.): 'Mitali's hair is long and black.' — 'hair' (collective, uncountable) takes a singular verb 'is'; correct.

 

• Option 3: 'One of the cars … is fifty years old.' — 'One of + plural noun' takes a singular verb; correct.

 

• Option 4: 'Sharon has shared her devastating grief after the sudden death of her 57-year-old brother.' — the compound adjective '57-year-old' is correctly hyphenated and singular; correct.

 

• Either/Neither — used for two; Any/None — used for more than two; Each — every one taken individually; Both — the two together (plural verb).

 

• Either of + plural noun + singular verb: Either of the boys is guilty.

 

NOTE

 

• Compound adjectives before a noun take a singular noun and hyphens: a five-year-old child, a ten-rupee note.

question: Identify the incorrect sentence.
option_1: Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated at the same time.
option_2: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is thousands of years old and has changed little over the centuries.
option_3: Folktales can be used to help children develop strong reading skills, study other cultures, and discover a love of stories.
option_4: Clothing is expensive because of the financial shakeup it received during the COVID-19 pandemic.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated at the same time.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The incorrect sentence is Option 1. The subject 'furniture' is an uncountable noun and always takes a singular verb.

 

• So 'Beautiful furniture make the house elegant and looks sophisticated' should be 'Beautiful furniture makes the house elegant and look sophisticated' (or '…makes the house look elegant and sophisticated').

 

• Also, the two verbs are not parallel: 'make' (plural form) and 'looks' (singular form) are inconsistent.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Correct — 'Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)' is singular and takes 'is … has changed'.

 

• Option 3: Correct — 'can be used to help children develop …, study …, and discover …' maintains parallelism.

 

• Option 4: Correct — 'Clothing' is uncountable/singular and takes 'is'; 'it received' agrees with it.

 

• Uncountable nouns that always take singular verbs: furniture, information, advice, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, scenery, poetry, news.

 

• They are never pluralised: ✗ furnitures, ✗ informations; use 'pieces of furniture', 'items of information'.

 

NOTE

 

• After 'make/let/help + object', use the bare infinitive: make the house look sophisticated (not 'looks').

question:
Choose the best option to replace the underlined part to improve the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution.'

They decided to go ahead with the new venture despite of the challenges.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In spite of.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Despite' is a preposition that is never followed by 'of'. The phrase 'despite of' is incorrect.

 

• The correct expressions are 'despite + noun' or 'in spite of + noun'.

 

• Correct sentence: They decided to go ahead with the new venture in spite of the challenges.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (In despite of): 'In despite of' — a non-standard, archaic expression; incorrect.

 

• Option 2 (In spite for): 'In spite for' — wrong preposition; the idiom is 'in spite of'.

 

• Option 4 (No substitution): 'No substitution' — incorrect because 'despite of' is grammatically wrong.

 

• Correct usage: Despite the rain, we played. / In spite of the rain, we played. / Despite the fact that it rained, we played.

 

• Both 'despite' and 'in spite of' express contrast (concession), like 'although', but they are followed by a noun/gerund, not a clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember: 'in spite of' — three words; 'despite' — one word, no 'of'.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

The pundit wrote a psalm on the goddess when he saw a miraculous incident on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.
option_1: A psalm on the goddess was being written by the pundit when a miraculous incident was seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.
option_2: A psalm on the goddess was written by the pundit when a miraculous incident was seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.
option_3: A psalm on the goddess was written by the pundit when a miraculous incident had been seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.
option_4: A psalm on the goddess has been written by the pundit when a miraculous incident seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A psalm on the goddess was written by the pundit when a miraculous incident was seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Active: 'The pundit wrote a psalm … when he saw a miraculous incident …' — both clauses are in the simple past tense.

 

• Passive of simple past: was/were + V3. So 'wrote a psalm' → 'a psalm was written by the pundit'; 'he saw a miraculous incident' → 'a miraculous incident was seen by him'.

 

• Correct passive: A psalm on the goddess was written by the pundit when a miraculous incident was seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'was being written' is the passive of past continuous (was writing) — tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'had been seen' is the passive of past perfect (had seen) — tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'has been written' (present perfect) and 'seen' without 'was' — wrong tense and incomplete verb; incorrect.

 

• Passive forms: Simple past — was/were + V3; Past continuous — was/were being + V3; Past perfect — had been + V3; Present perfect — has/have been + V3.

 

• In complex sentences, each clause with a transitive verb can be changed into passive, keeping its original tense.

 

NOTE

 

• The tense of the verb must never change while converting from active to passive voice.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

Somebody has broken the side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year.
option_1: The side lamps have been broken which were installed by the municipal corporation last year.
option_2: The side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year have been broken.
option_3: The side lamps which were being installed by the municipal corporation last year have been broken.
option_4: The side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year had been broken.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year have been broken.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Active: 'Somebody has broken the side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year.' — main verb in present perfect tense.

 

• Passive of present perfect: has/have been + V3. 'Somebody' (indefinite agent) is dropped in the passive.

 

• Correct passive: The side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year have been broken.

 

• The relative clause 'which had been installed …' is already in passive and stays attached to 'the side lamps'.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: The relative clause is separated from 'side lamps' and its tense is changed to 'were installed' — incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'were being installed' changes the tense of the relative clause (past continuous) — incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'had been broken' changes the main verb from present perfect to past perfect — incorrect.

 

• When the subject is indefinite (somebody, someone, people, they), the 'by + agent' phrase is omitted in the passive.

 

• Keep the relative clause immediately after the noun it describes to avoid ambiguity.

 

NOTE

 

• Present perfect passive: has/have + been + V3 (e.g., The work has been completed).

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

The culprit finally accepted that he had been guilty.
option_1: It was finally accepted by the culprit that he had been guilty.
option_2: It had been finally accepted by the culprit that was guilty.
option_3: That he had been guilty accepted the culprit finally.
option_4: That he had been guilty was accepted the culprit finally.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. It was finally accepted by the culprit that he had been guilty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Active: 'The culprit finally accepted that he had been guilty.' — The object here is the noun clause 'that he had been guilty'.

 

• When the object is a noun clause, the passive is usually formed with the introductory 'It': It + was + V3 + by + agent + that-clause.

 

• Correct passive: It was finally accepted by the culprit that he had been guilty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'It had been finally accepted … that was guilty' — wrong tense (past perfect) and the subject 'he' is missing in the that-clause; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'That he had been guilty accepted the culprit finally' — no passive verb (was accepted) and no 'by'; meaningless.

 

• Option 4: 'That he had been guilty was accepted the culprit finally' — 'by' is missing before 'the culprit'; incorrect.

 

• Noun clause as object → passive with 'It': They said that he was honest → It was said that he was honest.

 

• Alternatively the that-clause may itself become the subject: That he had been guilty was finally accepted by the culprit.

 

NOTE

 

• The tense of the reporting verb (accepted → was accepted) remains simple past.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

He said that he would not tolerate such nuissance in the office.
option_1: That such nuissance in the office would not be tolerated had been said by him.
option_2: It was said by him that such nuissance in the office would not be tolerated.
option_3: It had been said by him that such nuissance in the office would not be tolerated.
option_4: That such nuissance in the office would not be tolerating had been said by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It was said by him that such nuissance in the office would not be tolerated.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Active: 'He said that he would not tolerate such nuissance in the office.' — reporting verb 'said' is in simple past; the object is a noun clause.

 

• Passive of the main clause: It was said by him that … The noun-clause 'he would not tolerate such nuissance' also becomes passive: such nuissance … would not be tolerated.

 

• Correct passive: It was said by him that such nuissance in the office would not be tolerated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'had been said' — tense changed from simple past to past perfect; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'It had been said by him' — tense changed to past perfect; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'would not be tolerating' — ungrammatical passive form, and 'had been said' changes the tense; incorrect.

 

• Modal passive: would/should/could/can/will + be + V3 (would not tolerate → would not be tolerated).

 

• Note: the question sentence spells 'nuissance'; the standard spelling is nuisance (the options reproduce the question's spelling).

 

NOTE

 

• For object noun-clauses, the 'It + passive verb + that …' pattern is preferred in SSC questions.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

The wife advised the husband to maintain silence when she was practising yoga.
option_1: The husband was advised to maintain silence by the wife when yoga was practised by her.
option_2: The husband was advised by the wife to maintain silence when yoga was being practised by her.
option_3: The husband was advised by the wife to maintain silence by her when yoga was being practised.
option_4: The husband was advised to maintain silence when yoga was being practised by her by the wife.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The husband was advised by the wife to maintain silence when yoga was being practised by her.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Active: 'The wife advised the husband to maintain silence when she was practising yoga.'

 

• Main clause (simple past): 'advised the husband' → The husband was advised by the wife to maintain silence.

 

• Time clause (past continuous): 'she was practising yoga' → yoga was being practised by her.

 

• Correct passive: The husband was advised by the wife to maintain silence when yoga was being practised by her.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'when yoga was practised by her' — changes the past continuous into simple past; also 'by the wife' is misplaced; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'to maintain silence by her' — misplaced agent phrase that changes the meaning; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'by her by the wife' — two agent phrases jumbled at the end; illogical and incorrect.

 

• Past continuous passive: was/were + being + V3 (was practising → was being practised).

 

• The agent phrase ('by the wife') should be placed close to the verb it relates to (was advised by the wife).

 

NOTE

 

• Each clause keeps its own tense in the passive; do not merge or shift the agents.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

No decision has been taken yet.
option_1: They did not take any decision yet.
option_2: They have not taken any decision yet.
option_3: Nobody had taken any decision yet.
option_4: Nobody will take any decision yet.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. They have not taken any decision yet.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Passive: 'No decision has been taken yet.' — present perfect passive with an indefinite agent.

 

• Active of present perfect: has/have + V3. The implied agent is 'they'; 'No decision' becomes 'not … any decision'.

 

• Correct active: They have not taken any decision yet.

 

• 'Yet' is naturally used with the present perfect in negative sentences.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (They did not take any decision yet.): 'They did not take any decision yet' — simple past; the tense is changed and 'yet' does not suit simple past in standard usage; incorrect.

 

• Option 3 (Nobody had taken any decision yet.): 'Nobody had taken any decision yet' — past perfect; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 4 (Nobody will take any decision yet.): 'Nobody will take any decision yet' — future tense; tense and meaning changed; incorrect.

 

• When the passive has no agent, supply a suitable subject in the active: they, someone, people, we.

 

• 'No + noun' in passive → 'not … any + noun' in active: No work was done → They did not do any work.

 

NOTE

 

• Present perfect passive: has/have been + V3 ↔ Active: has/have + V3.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

Instructions will be given to the candidates.
option_2: Someone gives instructions to the candidates.
option_3: Someone will give instructions to the candidates.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Someone will give instructions to the candidates.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Passive: 'Instructions will be given to the candidates.' — simple future passive; the agent is not mentioned.

 

• Active of simple future: will + V1. Supply an indefinite subject 'Someone'.

 

• Correct active: Someone will give instructions to the candidates.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (The candidates give instructions.): 'The candidates give instructions' — wrong subject and wrong (present) tense; meaning reversed.

 

• Option 2 (Someone gives instructions to the candidates.): 'Someone gives instructions' — simple present; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 4 (Instructions will give the candidates.): 'Instructions will give the candidates' — makes 'instructions' the doer; illogical.

 

• Future passive: will/shall + be + V3 ↔ Active: will/shall + V1.

 

• The indirect object (the candidates) remains with 'to' when the direct object (instructions) is placed first.

 

NOTE

 

• Always check two things in voice questions: (1) tense unchanged, (2) doer and receiver correctly placed.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

What a beautiful painting has been made by her!
option_2: How beautiful painting she has made!
option_3: What a beautiful painting she has made!
option_4: She has been making a beautiful painting!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. What a beautiful painting she has made!

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Passive (exclamatory): 'What a beautiful painting has been made by her!' — present perfect passive.

 

• Active: the agent 'her' becomes the subject 'she', and the verb becomes 'has made'. The exclamatory structure 'What a + adjective + noun' is retained at the beginning.

 

• Correct active: What a beautiful painting she has made!

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (She makes a beautiful painting!): 'She makes a beautiful painting!' — simple present; tense changed and exclamatory form lost; incorrect.

 

• Option 2 (How beautiful painting she has made!): 'How beautiful painting she has made!' — 'How' is used with an adjective alone (How beautiful the painting is!); the article 'a' is missing; incorrect.

 

• Option 4 (She has been making a beautiful painting!): 'She has been making …' — present perfect continuous; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Exclamatory patterns: What + a/an + adjective + noun + subject + verb! (What a lovely day it is!) / How + adjective + subject + verb! (How lovely the day is!)

 

• Voice change does not change the sentence type — an exclamatory sentence remains exclamatory.

 

NOTE

 

• Present perfect: Active has made ↔ Passive has been made.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

Guests are not permitted to enter the kitchen.
option_1: They do not permit guests to enter the kitchen.
option_2: They did not permit guests to enter the kitchen.
option_3: They have not permitted guests to enter the kitchen.
option_4: They are not permitting guests to enter the kitchen.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. They do not permit guests to enter the kitchen.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Passive: 'Guests are not permitted to enter the kitchen.' — simple present passive; implied agent 'they'.

 

• Active of simple present: do/does not + V1.

 

• Correct active: They do not permit guests to enter the kitchen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'They did not permit' — simple past; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'They have not permitted' — present perfect; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'They are not permitting' — present continuous; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Simple present passive: is/am/are + V3 ↔ Active: V1/V1+s (negative: do/does not + V1).

 

• Verbs like permit, allow, advise, order, request take 'object + to-infinitive' (permit guests to enter).

 

NOTE

 

• In rules/notices, the passive (Guests are not permitted…) is common; its active form uses the general subject 'they'.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

The tourists were guided through the forest by a local ranger.
option_1: A local ranger is guiding the tourists through the forest.
option_2: A local ranger was guided through the forest by tourists.
option_3: A local ranger guides the tourists through the forest.
option_4: A local ranger guided the tourists through the forest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A local ranger guided the tourists through the forest.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Passive: 'The tourists were guided through the forest by a local ranger.' — simple past passive.

 

• Active: the agent 'a local ranger' becomes the subject; the verb becomes simple past 'guided'; 'the tourists' becomes the object.

 

• Correct active: A local ranger guided the tourists through the forest.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'is guiding' — present continuous; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Option 2: 'A local ranger was guided … by tourists' — roles reversed and still in passive; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'guides' — simple present; tense changed; incorrect.

 

• Simple past passive: was/were + V3 ↔ Active: V2.

 

• Steps: identify agent → make it subject → convert the verb into the same tense in active → make the passive subject the object.

 

NOTE

 

• Adverbial phrases (through the forest) remain unchanged during voice conversion.

question:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

Rimjhim said to Barsha, "Are you making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of you?"
option_1: Rimjhim asked Barsha was she making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.
option_2: Rimjhim asked Barsha if she was making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.
option_3: Rimjhim asked Barsha whether she had been making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.
option_4: Rimjhim asked Barsha whether she had made a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Rimjhim asked Barsha if she was making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The direct speech is an interrogative (yes/no) question, so the reporting verb 'said to' changes to 'asked' and the connective 'if/whether' is used.

 

• The question form is changed to statement form (subject + verb): 'Are you making' → 'she was making' (present continuous → past continuous).

 

• Pronouns: 'you' → 'she' (Barsha); 'in front of you' → 'in front of her'.

 

• Correct: Rimjhim asked Barsha if she was making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'asked Barsha was she making' — the connective 'if/whether' is missing and the interrogative word order is retained; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'had been making' — wrong tense change (present continuous → past continuous, not past perfect continuous); incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'had made' — wrong tense and meaning (completed action); incorrect.

 

• Yes/No questions: said to → asked; use if/whether; convert to assertive order; put a full stop at the end.

 

• Tense changes (past reporting verb): is/am/are + ing → was/were + ing; V1 → V2; V2 → had + V3.

 

NOTE

 

• Never keep the question mark or the question word order in indirect speech.

question:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

Risita says, “We were waving our hands at the passengers when the train passed.”
option_1: Risita says that they had been waving their hands at the passengers when the train passed.
option_2: Risita says that they were waving their hands at the passengers when the train had passed.
option_3: Risita says that they were waving their hands at the passengers when the train passed.
option_4: Risita says that they had been waving their hands at the passengers when the train had passed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Risita says that they were waving their hands at the passengers when the train passed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense. Hence, the tense of the reported speech does not change.

 

• Only the pronouns change: 'We' → 'they'; 'our' → 'their'. The connective 'that' is added.

 

• Correct: Risita says that they were waving their hands at the passengers when the train passed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'had been waving' — tense changed although the reporting verb is in the present; incorrect.

 

• Option 2: 'when the train had passed' — tense of the time clause changed unnecessarily; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: Both verbs changed into past perfect forms — incorrect when the reporting verb is present.

 

• Rule: If the reporting verb is in the present or future tense (says, will say), the tense of the reported speech remains unchanged.

 

• Tense changes apply only when the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked).

 

NOTE

 

• Universal truths, habitual facts and historical facts also do not change their tense, even with a past reporting verb.

question:
The following sentence has two blanks. Choose the most suitable set of prepositions from the given options to fill in the blanks and complete the sentence meaningfully:

She sat ____ the fireplace ____ keep warm.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. near, to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Near is a preposition of place meaning 'close to'. She sat near the fireplace — close to it.

 

• To in 'to keep warm' is part of the to-infinitive of purpose — it shows why she sat there.

 

• Complete sentence: She sat near the fireplace to keep warm.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (below, from): 'below, from' — one cannot sit 'below' a fireplace, and 'from keep warm' is ungrammatical.

 

• Option 2 (above, with): 'above, with' — sitting 'above' a fireplace is illogical, and 'with keep warm' is ungrammatical.

 

• Option 3 (above, with): 'above, with' — same as Option 2 (repeated in the paper); illogical and ungrammatical.

 

• Infinitive of purpose: to + V1 explains the reason for an action — He went to the market to buy vegetables.

 

• Prepositions of place: near (close to), beside (by the side of), by (next to), above (higher than), below (lower than), under (directly beneath).

 

NOTE

 

• 'In order to' can replace the infinitive of purpose: She sat near the fireplace in order to keep warm.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

She apologized and confessed that she had taken the documents without permission.
option_1: She confessed, "I took the documents without permission."
option_2: She apologized, "I have took the documents without permission."
option_3: She said, "I’m sorry. I had taken the documents without permission."
option_4: She said, "I’m sorry. I will not take the documents without permission."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She said, "I’m sorry. I had taken the documents without permission.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The indirect sentence contains two ideas: she apologized and she confessed that she had taken the documents without permission.

 

• An apology in direct speech is expressed by 'I’m sorry', and the confession is expressed as a statement in the first person.

 

• Among the options, Option 3 is the only one that conveys both the apology and the confession: She said, "I’m sorry. I had taken the documents without permission."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: It conveys the confession but omits the apology entirely; incomplete.

 

• Option 2: 'I have took' is ungrammatical — the correct form is 'have taken'; also the apology is missing.

 

• Option 4: 'I will not take the documents' changes the meaning into a promise about the future, not a confession about the past.

 

• Converting indirect to direct: identify the reporting verb (apologized/confessed → said, "I’m sorry…"), change pronouns back to first/second person, and reverse the tense backshift where appropriate.

 

• Words like apologized, thanked, wished, greeted, congratulated in indirect speech are expressed through sentences such as 'I’m sorry', 'Thank you', 'Good morning', 'Congratulations' in direct speech.

 

NOTE

 

• Strictly, the backshift 'had taken' would become 'took/have taken' in direct speech; however, in the given options, Option 3 is the only complete and grammatical choice, as per the official key.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

The technician explained that the system had crashed due to a power surge.
option_1: The technician explained, "The system had crashed due to a power surge."
option_2: The technician said, "The system have crashed due to a power surge."
option_3: The technician explained, "The system has crash due to a power surge."
option_4: The technician explained, "The system crashes due to a power surge."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The technician explained, "The system had crashed due to a power surge.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indirect: 'The technician explained that the system had crashed due to a power surge.'

 

• In direct speech, the reporting verb 'explained' is retained with a comma and inverted commas, and the reported statement is given in the speaker’s own words.

 

• Option 1 keeps the correct reporting verb and a grammatically complete reported statement: The technician explained, "The system had crashed due to a power surge."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'The system have crashed' — subject–verb disagreement ('system' is singular: has, not have); incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'has crash' — wrong verb form (should be 'has crashed'); incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'The system crashes' — simple present changes the meaning into a habitual action; incorrect.

 

• Backshift reversal (indirect → direct): had + V3 → V2 / has + V3; was/were → is/am/are; would → will; could → can.

 

• Singular collective/single nouns like 'system' take singular verbs: has, is, was.

 

NOTE

 

• The most natural direct form would be "The system has crashed / crashed due to a power surge"; among the given options, only Option 1 is grammatically correct and faithful to the original.

question:
Choose the most suitable preposition from the given options to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

My house is just one-kilometre ____ the beach.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. from.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Distance is measured from a reference point. Hence, 'one kilometre from the beach'.

 

• Complete sentence: My house is just one-kilometre from the beach.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (to): 'to the beach' shows direction/destination, not distance from a point; incorrect here.

 

• Option 2 (of): 'of the beach' — 'within one kilometre of' is possible, but 'one kilometre of the beach' is incorrect.

 

• Option 3 (till): 'till' is used for time (till evening), not for distance or place.

 

• Distance expressions: far from, away from, a mile from, at a distance of, within two kilometres of.

 

• Till/until refer to time; to/up to refer to place limits (from Delhi to Agra).

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the pair: from (starting point) … to (end point): The school is 2 km from my house; I walk to school.

question:
Choose the most suitable preposition from the given options to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

We heard the unfortunate news ____ the radio.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. over.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• We hear news over (or on) the radio/telephone — the preposition 'over' is used for communication through broadcast or telephone lines.

 

• Complete sentence: We heard the unfortunate news over the radio.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (in): 'in the radio' would mean physically inside the device; incorrect.

 

• Option 2 (from): 'from the radio' is not idiomatic in this sense.

 

• Option 4 (at): 'at the radio' is incorrect; 'at' is used for a point/place.

 

• Idiomatic usage: over/on the radio, over/on the phone, on television, on the internet, in the newspaper.

 

• He spoke to me over the phone. / I heard it on the radio.

 

NOTE

 

• In SSC, when both 'on' and 'over' are possible for radio/phone, choose whichever appears in the options.

question:
The following sentence has two blanks. Choose the most suitable set of prepositions from the given options to fill in the blanks and complete the sentence meaningfully:

The book is divided ____ five parts and dedicated ____ the author’s parents.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. into, to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Divided into is the fixed expression used when something is split into parts: The book is divided into five parts.

 

• Dedicated to is used when a work is devoted to someone as a mark of respect/affection: dedicated to the author’s parents.

 

• Complete sentence: The book is divided into five parts and dedicated to the author’s parents.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (among, to): 'divided among' is used when something is shared between people, not split into parts; incorrect.

 

• Option 2 (into, for): 'dedicated for' is incorrect; 'dedicate' takes 'to'.

 

• Option 4 (in, to): 'divided in five parts' is non-standard; 'divide into' is the correct phrasal combination.

 

• Divide into (parts), divide among (more than two people), divide between (two people), divide by (mathematics).

 

• Dedicate to / devote to / committed to — each takes 'to'.

 

NOTE

 

• Fixed prepositions after verbs and adjectives are frequently tested in SSC; learn them as pairs.

question:
The following sentence has two blanks. Choose the most suitable set of prepositions from the given options to fill in the blanks and complete the sentence meaningfully:

The policy is inconsistent ____ the company's values and incompatible ____ our long-term goals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. with, with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Inconsistent with — the adjective 'inconsistent' is followed by the preposition with.

 

• Incompatible with — the adjective 'incompatible' is also followed by with.

 

• Complete sentence: The policy is inconsistent with the company's values and incompatible with our long-term goals.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (with, to): 'incompatible to' is incorrect; the correct preposition is 'with'.

 

• Option 3 (at, with): 'inconsistent at' is incorrect.

 

• Option 4 (for, with): 'inconsistent for' is incorrect.

 

• Adjectives with 'with': consistent with, compatible with, familiar with, angry with (a person), content with, identical with/to.

 

• Adjectives with 'to': similar to, equal to, inferior to, superior to, averse to.

 

NOTE

 

• The opposites also take the same prepositions: consistent/inconsistent with, compatible/incompatible with.

question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

She said that by the time the guests arrived, the decorations would already have been completed.
option_1: She said, "By the time the guests arrive, the decorations will already have been completed."
option_2: She said, "By the time the guests will arrive, the decorations would’ve been completed."
option_3: She said, "By the time the guests would arrive, the decorations would be complete."
option_4: She said, "By the time the guests arrived, the decorations will already have completed."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She said, "By the time the guests arrive, the decorations will already have been completed.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indirect: 'She said that by the time the guests arrived, the decorations would already have been completed.'

 

• Reversing the backshift: arrived (past) → arrive (present); would have been completed → will have been completed (future perfect passive).

 

• In a time clause ('by the time …'), English uses the present tense for future reference, not 'will'.

 

• Correct direct: She said, "By the time the guests arrive, the decorations will already have been completed."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'By the time the guests will arrive' — future tense is not used in a time clause; also 'would’ve been' is not reversed; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'would arrive … would be complete' — the backshift is not reversed; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'arrived … will already have completed' — tense mismatch and active 'have completed' wrongly replaces the passive; incorrect.

 

• Time clauses (when, as soon as, by the time, before, after, until) take the present tense for future meaning: I will call you when I reach home.

 

• Future perfect passive: will have been + V3.

 

NOTE

 

• Direct ↔ Indirect: will ↔ would; will have been ↔ would have been; present ↔ past.

question:
Which word can best replace highlighted?

Bailey highlighted Marsh’s impressive performance against England and his ability to turn a game around.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Emphasized.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Highlight (verb) means to draw special attention to something; to emphasize it. (प्रकाश डालना / ज़ोर देना)

 

• Bailey drew special attention to Marsh’s impressive performance, i.e. he emphasized it.

 

• 'Emphasized' conveys the exact sense of 'giving prominence', which makes it the best replacement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Mentioned): 'Mentioned' means merely referred to in passing — it lacks the idea of special emphasis.

 

• Option 3 (Displayed): 'Displayed' means exhibited or showed physically — not used for pointing out qualities in speech.

 

• Option 4 (Stressed): 'Stressed' is close in meaning, but the official key and standard dictionary equivalent of 'highlight' is 'emphasize'; 'stress' is more often used for importance or pressure.

 

• Synonyms of highlight (verb): emphasize, underline, spotlight, accentuate, point up, foreground. Antonyms: downplay, understate, ignore, play down.

 

NOTE

 

• Noun 'highlight' = the most outstanding part (the highlight of the match).

question: What is the antonym of "Impecunious?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wealthy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Impecunious means having little or no money; poor. (निर्धन / कंगाल)

 

• Its antonym is Wealthy — having a great deal of money; rich. (धनी)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Broke): 'Broke' (informal) means having no money — a synonym.

 

• Option 3 (Poor): 'Poor' is a direct synonym.

 

• Option 4 (Destitute): 'Destitute' means extremely poor, lacking basic necessities — a synonym.

 

• Synonyms of impecunious: penniless, needy, indigent, impoverished, hard up, insolvent. Antonyms: wealthy, rich, affluent, prosperous, opulent, well-off.

 

NOTE

 

• Root: Latin 'pecunia' = money; 'im-' = not. Related: pecuniary (relating to money).

question: What is the antonym of "Ebullient"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Depressed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ebullient means cheerful and full of energy; exuberant. (उत्साही / जोश से भरा)

 

• Its antonym is Depressed — in low spirits, sad and lacking energy. (उदास)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Enthusiastic): 'Enthusiastic' means full of eager interest — a synonym.

 

• Option 3 (Animated): 'Animated' means lively and full of life — a synonym.

 

• Option 4 (Joyous): 'Joyous' means full of happiness — a synonym.

 

• Synonyms of ebullient: exuberant, buoyant, effervescent, bubbly, vivacious. Antonyms: depressed, dejected, gloomy, subdued, apathetic.

 

NOTE

 

• Noun: ebullience. Literal meaning: 'boiling over' (Latin 'ebullire').

question:
Which word is closest in meaning to inclusion?

Kohli’s inclusion would give India more balance and depth in the squad.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Addition.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Inclusion means the action of being included or added within a group or structure. (शामिल किया जाना)

 

• Kohli’s inclusion (i.e., his addition to the squad) would give India more balance and depth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Entry): 'Entry' means the act of coming in / access — it does not specifically mean being included in a team.

 

• Option 3 (Involvement): 'Involvement' means participation or engagement in an activity — broader and less precise.

 

• Option 4 (Presence): 'Presence' means the state of being present — it does not denote the act of adding someone.

 

• Synonyms of inclusion: addition, incorporation, insertion, admission. Antonyms: exclusion, omission, removal, elimination.

 

NOTE

 

• Related forms: include (verb), inclusive (adj.), inclusively (adv.).

question: What is the antonym of "Sybaritic"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Spartan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sybaritic means fond of sensuous luxury or pleasure; self-indulgent. (विलासी)

 

• Its antonym is Spartan — showing or characterized by austerity, simplicity and a lack of comfort or luxury. (सादा / कठोर अनुशासन वाला)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (Luxurious): 'Luxurious' — a synonym of sybaritic.

 

• Option 3 (Pampered): 'Pampered' — indulged with every comfort; a synonym.

 

• Option 4 (Sensual): 'Sensual' — relating to physical pleasures; a synonym.

 

• Origin: Sybaris — an ancient Greek city in Italy famous for luxury; Sparta — a Greek city-state famous for strict discipline and simple living.

 

• Synonyms of sybaritic: hedonistic, self-indulgent, voluptuous, luxurious. Antonyms: ascetic, austere, spartan, abstemious.

 

NOTE

 

• Eponymous adjectives from places are common in SSC: spartan, laconic (Laconia), sybaritic (Sybaris).

question: What is the antonym of "Acerbic"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Saccharine.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Acerbic means sharp and forthright; bitter or harsh in tone (especially of speech or humour). (कटु / तीखा)

 

• Its antonym is Saccharine — excessively sweet or sentimental. (अत्यधिक मीठा)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (Sardonic): 'Sardonic' means grimly mocking or cynical — a synonym.

 

• Option 2 (Sharp): 'Sharp' — a synonym in the sense of cutting or biting.

 

• Option 3 (Scathing): 'Scathing' means severely critical — a synonym.

 

• Synonyms of acerbic: caustic, biting, mordant, trenchant, sarcastic, acrid. Antonyms: sweet, mild, gentle, kind, saccharine.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Saccharine' is also the name of an artificial sweetener (saccharin — spelt without the final 'e').

question: Which of the following is NOT a meaning of the homonym ‘recess’?
option_2: A break or pause in proceedings, especially in school or court
option_3: A remote, secluded, or inner part of something
option_4: A hollow space or indentation in a wall
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Slow backward movement and disappearance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The homonym 'recess' has these meanings: (i) a break or pause in proceedings (school/court), (ii) a remote, secluded or inner part, (iii) a hollow space or indentation in a wall.

 

• 'Slow backward movement and disappearance' is NOT a meaning of 'recess'; it describes recession/receding (the act of moving back or withdrawing).

 

• Hence, Option 1 is the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: A break or pause in proceedings, especially in school or court — a valid meaning (e.g., the court is in recess).

 

• Option 3: A remote, secluded or inner part of something — a valid meaning (e.g., the recesses of the mind).

question:
From the given alternatives, select the correct indirect narration of the given direct narration.

Gagan said, "Alas! The king and musician is no more!"
option_1: Gagan said alas and said that the king and musician was no more.
option_2: Gagan exclaimed sorrowfully that the king and musician was no more.
option_3: Gagan exclaimed that the king and musician had no more.
option_4: Gagan exclaimed sadly that the king and musician were no more.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Gagan exclaimed sorrowfully that the king and musician was no more.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Alas!' expresses sorrow/grief. In indirect speech, the interjection is removed and the reporting verb becomes 'exclaimed sorrowfully / exclaimed with sorrow'.

 

• 'The king and musician' refers to one person (the article 'the' is used only once), so it takes a singular verb: 'is' → was.

 

• Correct: Gagan exclaimed sorrowfully that the king and musician was no more.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'Gagan said alas and said that…' — interjections are not retained in indirect speech; clumsy and incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'had no more' — changes the meaning; 'is no more' (is dead) → 'was no more', not 'had no more'.

 

• Option 4: 'were no more' — plural verb wrongly treats one person (the king and musician) as two.

 

• Article rule: The king and the musician (two persons) → plural verb; The king and musician (one person holding both roles) → singular verb.

 

• Exclamations: Alas! → exclaimed with sorrow; Hurrah! → exclaimed with joy; Bravo! → applauded; What/How + adjective → exclaimed that it was very…

 

NOTE

 

• 'Is no more' is an idiom meaning 'has died'.

question:
From the given alternatives, select the correct direct narration of the given indirect narration.

Samaira told Pankaj that he had proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job.
option_1: Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job."
option_2: Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proudly shows off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job."
option_3: Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proud show off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job."
option_4: Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he was just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indirect: 'Samaira told Pankaj that he had proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he had just bought …'

 

• In the direct form, the reporting verb 'told' becomes 'said to', the reported words are placed in inverted commas, and the past perfect of the reported action is reversed to the simple past: had showed off → showed off.

 

• The subordinate clause 'he had just bought' correctly remains in the past perfect as it refers to an earlier action.

 

• Correct direct: Samaira said to Pankaj, "He proudly showed off the brand new bicycle he had just bought with his hard-earned money from his part-time job."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'He proudly shows off' — simple present; wrong tense reversal and tense inconsistency with 'had just bought'.

 

• Option 3: 'He proud show off' — adjective 'proud' used instead of the adverb 'proudly', and wrong verb form; ungrammatical.

 

• Option 4: 'he was just bought' — passive form wrongly makes the bicycle-buyer the object; ungrammatical.

 

• Indirect → Direct: told → said to; had + V3 → V2 (or has/have + V3); that → removed; add inverted commas and capitalise the first word of the quote.

 

• 'Show off' (phrasal verb) = to display proudly; its past form is 'showed off' (standard V3: shown).

 

NOTE

 

• An adverb (proudly) modifies a verb; an adjective (proud) modifies a noun — a common trap in options.

question:
In the following sentence, a part of the sentence is bolded. Choose the correct alternative that best improves the bolded part.

Unless the regulators do not intervene in the proposed corporate merger, the resulting monopoly will stifle all local competition and innovation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Unless the regulators.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Unless' already means 'if not'. Using 'not' after 'unless' creates a double negative — 'Unless the regulators do not intervene' is incorrect.

 

• Correct improvement: Unless the regulators intervene in the proposed corporate merger, the resulting monopoly will stifle all local competition and innovation.

 

• Meaning: If the regulators do not intervene, a monopoly will result.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (If the regulators): 'If the regulators intervene' reverses the meaning — intervention would prevent, not cause, the monopoly.

 

• Option 2 (Unless the regulator): 'Unless the regulator' — changes the plural 'regulators' to singular; the verb 'intervene' would then need to be 'intervenes'.

 

• Option 3 (Provided the regulators): 'Provided the regulators' means 'on condition that they intervene' — reverses the intended meaning.

 

• Unless = if not; Until = up to the time when (time). Neither is followed by 'not' in the same clause.

 

• Correct: Unless you work hard, you will fail. ✗ Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.

 

NOTE

 

• In conditional sentences with 'unless', the main clause usually takes 'will + V1' and the unless-clause takes the simple present.

question:
In the following sentence, a part of the sentence is bolded. Choose the correct alternative that best improves the bolded part.

I will depart immediately, mustn't I, to avoid missing the final flight connection to the international conference in London?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I must depart immediately.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence ends with the question tag 'mustn't I'. A question tag must match the auxiliary/modal of the main clause.

 

• Since the tag uses 'must', the main clause must contain 'must': I must depart immediately, mustn't I, …

 

• After a modal, the bare infinitive (V1) is used: must + depart.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (I must have depart immediately): 'I must have depart' — after 'must have' the past participle (departed) is needed; also changes meaning; incorrect.

 

• Option 2 (I must been depart immediately): 'I must been depart' — ungrammatical combination.

 

• Option 3 (I must had depart immediately): 'I must had depart' — modals are never followed by 'had'; ungrammatical.

 

• Question tag rules: positive statement → negative tag (I must go, mustn't I?); negative statement → positive tag (He can't swim, can he?).

 

• The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement: will → won’t, can → can’t, must → mustn’t.

 

NOTE

 

• 'I am…' takes the tag 'aren't I?' (not 'amn't I').

question:
In the following sentence, a part of the sentence is bolded. Choose the correct alternative that best improves the bolded part.

The pilot had been more vigilant regarding the weather reports, the emergency landing could have been successfully averted.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Had the pilot been.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence expresses an unreal past condition (third conditional): if the pilot had been more vigilant, the landing could have been averted.

 

• The 'if' can be omitted by inverting the subject and 'had': Had the pilot been more vigilant, …

 

• Correct sentence: Had the pilot been more vigilant regarding the weather reports, the emergency landing could have been successfully averted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (If the pilot was): 'If the pilot was' — second conditional (present/future unreal); does not match 'could have been' in the main clause.

 

• Option 2 (Should the pilot be): 'Should the pilot be' — used for possible future conditions; tense mismatch.

 

• Option 4 (Was the pilot being): 'Was the pilot being' — ungrammatical as a conditional inversion.

 

• Third conditional: If + had + V3, would/could/might + have + V3.

 

• Inversions: Had I known = If I had known; Were I you = If I were you; Should you need = If you should need.

 

NOTE

 

• The given bolded part lacked 'if' or inversion, making it a statement instead of a condition — hence it needed improvement.

question:

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence:

The supervisor ordered the peon to post those letters.
option_1: The supervisor said to the peon, "Post these letters."
option_2: The supervisor said to the peon, "Post those letters."
option_3: The supervisor said to the peon, "Posted these letters."
option_4: The supervisor said to the peon, "You have to post those letters."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The supervisor said to the peon, "Post these letters.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indirect: 'The supervisor ordered the peon to post those letters.' — an imperative (command).

 

• In direct speech: ordered → said to; the to-infinitive becomes an imperative (Post …).

 

• The demonstrative 'those' (indirect) changes back to 'these' (direct), since the letters are near the speaker at the time of speaking.

 

• Correct: The supervisor said to the peon, "Post these letters."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: 'Post those letters' — 'those' is not changed back to 'these'; incorrect as per the rules of narration.

 

• Option 3: 'Posted these letters' — past tense instead of the imperative; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'You have to post those letters' — not an imperative and 'those' is not reversed; incorrect.

 

• Direct ↔ Indirect changes: this ↔ that, these ↔ those, here ↔ there, now ↔ then, today ↔ that day, tomorrow ↔ the next day.

 

• Imperatives: said to → ordered/commanded/requested/advised + to-infinitive.

 

NOTE

 

• Negative imperative: said, "Don’t go" → forbade/told … not to go.

option_1: She said that she was sorry but she cannot help him.
option_2: She apologised and said that she could not help you.
option_3: She apologised and told him that she could not help him.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She apologised and told him that she could not help him.

• Pronoun 'you' → him (the listener); 'I' → she.

 

• Tense: 'cannot' (can) → could not.

 

• Correct: She apologised and told him that she could not help him.

• Option 2: 'could not help you' — 'you' is not changed to 'him'; incorrect.

 

• Option 4: 'could not help you' — the pronoun 'you' is retained wrongly; incorrect.

 

• Modal changes: can → could, may → might, will → would, shall → should; must → had to (or must).

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.

“How long have you been waiting for me?” he asked his friend.
option_1: He asked his friend how long had he been waiting for him.
option_2: He asked his friend how long he has been waiting for him.
option_3: He asked his friend how long he had been waiting for me.
option_4: He asked his friend how long he had been waiting for him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He asked his friend how long he had been waiting for him.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The direct speech is a wh-question ('How long have you been waiting for me?'). The question word 'how long' is used as the connective and the sentence is converted into assertive word order (subject + verb).

 

• Tense: present perfect continuous (have been waiting) → past perfect continuous (had been waiting).

 

• Pronouns: 'you' → he (the friend); 'me' → him (the speaker).

 

• Correct: He asked his friend how long he had been waiting for him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 'how long had he been waiting' — interrogative word order retained; incorrect.

 

• Option 2: 'he has been waiting' — tense not changed after the past reporting verb 'asked'; incorrect.

 

• Option 3: 'waiting for me' — 'me' not changed to 'him'; incorrect.

 

• Wh-questions in indirect speech: said to → asked; the wh-word itself joins the clauses; no 'if/whether'; no question mark; subject comes before verb.

 

• Tense change: have/has been + V-ing → had been + V-ing.

 

NOTE

 

• Pronouns in reported speech follow the SON rule: 1st person → subject of reporting verb; 2nd person → object of reporting verb; 3rd person → no change.

question:
In the following question, the first and last parts of the sentence (1 and 6) are given. The rest of the sentence is split into four parts and named P, Q, R, and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct.

1. Chronic pollution in

P. respiratory health and

Q. major cities affects

R. chronic diseases globally

S. contributes to rising rates of

6. among the urban population.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. QPSR.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Start: 1. Chronic pollution in → Q. major cities affects (pollution in major cities affects …).

 

• Object of 'affects': P. respiratory health and.

 

• Second verb (parallel with 'affects'): S. contributes to rising rates of.

 

• Object of 'rates of': R. chronic diseases globally → 6. among the urban population.

 

• Correct sentence: Chronic pollution in major cities affects respiratory health and contributes to rising rates of chronic diseases globally among the urban population. — QPSR.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (RSQP): 'RSQP' — 'Chronic pollution in chronic diseases globally…' — meaningless.

 

• Option 3 (SRQP): 'SRQP' — 'Chronic pollution in contributes to…' — ungrammatical.

 

• Option 4 (QSRP): 'QSRP' — 'affects contributes to…' — two verbs without a connector; ungrammatical.

 

• Parallel structure: Subject + verb 1 (affects) + object + and + verb 2 (contributes to) + object.

 

• 'Contribute to' (take preposition 'to') + noun: contributes to rising rates.

 

NOTE

 

• In P–Q–R–S questions, first link the given first part (1) with a grammatically compatible part.

question:
Given below are four jumbled parts of a sentence. Select the option that gives their correct order and forms a meaningful sentence.

A. spending a full day away from social media

B.  after a long period of feeling overwhelmed

C. finally regain my focus and mental clarity

D. and other digital distractions enabled me to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. ADCB.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Subject (gerund phrase): A. spending a full day away from social media + D. and other digital distractions enabled me to.

 

• 'enabled me to' requires a bare verb: C. finally regain my focus and mental clarity.

 

• End with the time phrase: B. after a long period of feeling overwhelmed.

 

• Correct sentence: Spending a full day away from social media and other digital distractions enabled me to finally regain my focus and mental clarity after a long period of feeling overwhelmed. — ADCB.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (ABCD): 'ABCD' — 'social media after a long period… finally regain… and other digital distractions' — illogical.

 

• Option 3 (CDAB): 'CDAB' — begins with 'finally regain…' — no subject; ungrammatical.

 

• Option 4 (DABC): 'DABC' — begins with 'and other digital distractions…' — cannot start with 'and'.

 

• Gerund as subject: a gerund phrase (Spending a full day …) takes a singular verb (enabled).

 

• Enable + object + to-infinitive: enabled me to regain.

 

NOTE

 

• The part ending with 'to' must be followed by a part beginning with a base verb (regain).

question:

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ACBD.

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. Because of this design, the system could drastically reduce travel time between major cities.

B. The Hyperloop is a high-speed transportation system that uses magnetic levitation inside low-pressure tubes to travel at very high speeds.

C. To turn this idea into reality, several companies are actively working on building and testing prototypes.

D. If these efforts succeed, the system would represent a revolutionary step in sustainable mass transportation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BACD.

• B introduces the topic and describes the Hyperloop's design.

 

• A follows — 'Because of this design, the system could drastically reduce travel time…' (refers back to B).

 

• C — 'To turn this idea into reality, several companies are actively working…'.

 

• D concludes — 'If these efforts succeed, the system would represent a revolutionary step…'.

 

• Correct order: BACD.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (CBDA): 'CBDA' — C refers to 'this idea', which needs an earlier introduction; cannot be first.

 

• Option 3 (DABC): 'DABC' — D ('these efforts') cannot open the paragraph.

 

• Option 4 (ADCB): 'ADCB' — A ('this design') cannot open the paragraph.

 

• The Hyperloop concept was popularised by Elon Musk in 2013; it involves pods travelling in low-pressure tubes using magnetic levitation.

 

• In India, IIT Madras (through its Avishkar Hyperloop team) has developed a hyperloop test track.

 

NOTE

 

• Demonstratives like 'this design', 'this idea', 'these efforts' link each sentence to the previous one.
